video.title: He Watched This Channel and Started a $2,600/Week Side Hustle

summary: Tim describes testing a mobile RC construction play experience at fairs and private events, then preparing a permanent store with construction and rock-crawling zones. He shares session prices, event costs, startup spending, early sales, and the software he built in Replit to manage sessions and other operations. The store is a larger, less-proven expansion, with memberships and an outdoor course planned. The main takeaway is that event testing helped him learn about demand and operations before committing to a permanent location, though several store projections remain estimates.

ideas.name: Mobile RC construction play trailer
ideas.one_liner: A trailer-based sand pit where children and adults pay to operate remote-controlled construction machines at fairs, festivals, and private events.
ideas.business_model: Per-session play fees, private-party bookings, and paid appearances at public or corporate events.
ideas.customer: Families, children, adults interested in construction or RC vehicles, and event organizers.
ideas.problem: People want an unusual, hands-on activity at fairs, parties, and family events; the transcript does not state this as a customer-research finding.
ideas.offer: Timed use of RC excavators, front loaders, a crane, trucks, and other vehicles in a sand pit.

pricing.model: Timed sessions, private-event bookings, and event appearance fees.

pricing.notes: The $5 session price is equivalent to $1 per minute. Tim says the store will use a different pricing model.

acquisition_channels.details: No marketplace was named. The business booked space at county fairs and festivals; event fees and access requirements varied.
Tim spoke with vendors and attendees at events. A meeting at a local pizza pub event led to a Choice Hotels marketing contact inviting the business to a tailgate.

quote.text: We talked to everybody at every event because we've learned so much.
quote.speaker: Tim

acquisition_channels.details: People who saw the trailer at one fair recognized it at later fairs; a Choice Hotels contact approached Tim after his children played.

quote.text: Hey, we have this big tailgate. You guys should We'd love to have you.
quote.speaker: Tim

acquisition_channels.details: Handed out branded stickers and fridge magnets at events. Tim says they were used to promote the logo and website.

quote.text: We made them a magnet, so you could just put them on your fridge.
quote.speaker: Tim

ideas.delivery: Tim and his wife run the trailer at events. They set up a sand pit, hand out remotes, take payments, answer questions, monitor session times, change batteries, and right vehicles that flip over. A customer can use different machines during their paid session.
unit_economics_claims: Tim says 1,700 sessions sold at $5 each over the summer and seven private parties booked at $399 for two hours.
He says changing from $5 for 10 minutes to $5 for 5 minutes doubled the business.
Fair fees were reported as $100 to $550 per week.
The first fair sold 10 sessions and generated about $50 in revenue, which Tim says was effectively lost to food bought by his daughter and her friend.
He reports typical bad-day revenue of $200 to $300 and best-day revenue of $800.
He reports about $2,600 in revenue at a five-day fair.
The trailer version cost about $10,000 to $11,000 to start.
tools: Custom session-tracking and POS app built in Replit
RC excavators, front loaders, crane, trucks, and other vehicles
Trailer, sand pit, remotes, batteries, and session display
ideas.startup_cost: Tim estimates about $10,000 to $11,000 for the trailer version, including a $6,000 trailer, machines, four-wheel-drive vehicles, and marketing materials.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; Tim says it took roughly six to eight months to break even.

acquisition.how: Event attendance, networking, and in-person promotion require a person. In-person sales and event relationships are not unattended software tasks.

onboarding.how: The app records a customer's name, optional email, and session length, but a person still interacts with the customer and starts the sale.

delivery.how: A person must set up and operate the physical trailer, hand out remotes, change batteries, answer questions, and reset flipped vehicles.

billing.how: The custom app supports sales, but staff take payment and handle the customer interaction.

support.how: Staff answer questions, explain the activity, and manage equipment and session issues in person.

uk_applicability.notes: The event-based activity could work in the UK, but venue access, event fees, insurance, seasonal weather, and local demand would need adapting. The reported US fair prices and customer economics do not establish UK pricing.

risks: Tim says the trailer walls were too high for passers-by to see the activity, and that it could look like an ordinary trailer among other event vendors.
Some visitors thought the business sold the machines, so the offer needed explaining.
Demand at outdoor events depends on crowd size and weather; a high event fee does not guarantee a good result.
Parents sometimes thought the session price was too expensive.
The RC cars flipped often, creating staff work, and the first trailer layout did not work well for both operators inside.
Machines ran through their batteries during a very busy paid event.
Tim says a pair of dump trucks did not work in the sand pit as designed.

The transcript says customer names and emails are retained for marketing but does not describe consent or another legal basis. For UK marketing, the business would need to follow PECR and data-protection requirements.

tactics.name: Test the idea at events before committing to a store
steps: Build a mobile version and book events to see whether families will pay.
Track sales and learn which event crowds fit the activity.
Use visitor questions and event recognition as signals for whether a permanent venue could have demand.

quote.text: What a good way to prove the demand first? Yeah. With $6,000 or 10, 10,000.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Shorten sessions when parents do not want to wait
steps: Start by selling timed sessions.
Notice whether the session length creates friction for parents waiting nearby.
Tim changed from $5 for 10 minutes to $5 for 5 minutes and says the change doubled the business.

quote.text: I convinced my wife that we needed to go to $5 for 5 minutes. She thought we both thought it was too expensive, but it doubled our business.
quote.speaker: Tim

tactics.name: Make the activity visible from the walkway
steps: Design the pit so passers-by can see the machines operating.
Tim says his trailer wall was too high and made the activity hard to see.
Use clear signage to explain that visitors pay to play rather than buy the machines.

quote.text: Had I made it lower, people just passing by would have seen more of what was going on.
quote.speaker: Tim

tactics.name: Use event vendors and customers to create partnerships
steps: Talk with other vendors and attendees at each event.
Explain the activity and answer questions about parties and bookings.
Follow up on event conversations; Tim says a local event led to a Choice Hotels tailgate booking.

quote.text: We talked to everybody at every event because we've learned so much.
quote.speaker: Tim

tactics.name: Give visitors something useful to keep
steps: Try branded stickers for children.
Give parents branded magnets with the logo and website so they can keep the contact details on a fridge.
Track which event handouts get a positive response.

quote.text: We made them a magnet, so you could just put them on your fridge.
quote.speaker: Tim

tactics.name: Automate session timing with a visible countdown
steps: Record the customer's name and session length in the app.
Show the session on a monitor with a short setup buffer.
Change the display color and flash it as time runs out so parents can help enforce the end of the session.

quote.text: As it gets closer to the end of the time, it changes colors to warn them and it will start to flash.
quote.speaker: Tim

tactics.name: Build software by testing and revising
steps: Tim says to be patient and use planning mode to discuss the app before asking the tool to build.
Test the result, report issues, and repeat the cycle.
Add features as operational needs become clear.

steps: Track sessions, sales, customer accounts, inventory, events, and event requests.
Use the same system for gift cards, memberships, and the newsletter.

evidence_quality.rationale: Tim is a first-hand operator and gives concrete operating details, event prices, setup costs, and sales examples. Some figures are approximate, several costs and forecasts are not fully specified, and the permanent store and planned add-ons had not yet been proven in the transcript. The host's store profit scenario is explicitly hypothetical.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host reads promotional ads for Beehiiv and HighLevel and promotes TK Owners. These are promotional segments, not business ideas.
